news.title: Miranda Kerr’s bison diet is everything wrong with podcasting
news.text:
Given that she is a model, a multi-millionaire, the ex-wife of Orlando Bloom and starts her day at 5am with sun salutations, dry brushing and celery juice, I have not spent much of my life comparing myself with Miranda Kerr. 

Now 43 and a skincare mogul, Kerr has been at the vanguard of the toxic wellness culture of the last decade, famous for her absurd morning routines and “360-degree holistic” approach to health, which is laughably unrealistic and whose benefits are spurious. So I am perplexed to have found myself for the past two hours reading about “oxalates” – a term I had never heard until this week – and spinach and kale, leaves I hitherto believed healthy and I now understand are to be avoided if I want to commit to the glowing, parasite-free purity of Kerr.

This week, Kerr (13.8m Instagram followers) appeared on the podcast of former reality star Kristin Cavallari (4.9m Instagram followers) to promote her brand, Kora Organics. Chief among the mind-numbing conversation topics was her diet: she doesn’t eat eggs: “I do protein… bison, venison, lamb…” No sushi, because of “parasites”, no wheat, no dairy. But caviar is fine, and when asked if she eats carbs, the reply was: “I really eat a lot of squash, carrots, parsnips”, but “I don’t eat kale”. Or spinach. My patience and IQ atrophied just watching it.

The world – or at least millennial women like me who like to believe ourselves capable of at least some critical thinking – is used to Kerr’s pseudo-scientific bullshit by now, so her diet, which sounds alarmingly restrictive, is of little surprise. The really outrageous part is the response of the host. Marvelling at Kerr, and I suppose her venerable commitment to all this, Cavallari said: “So you really are, like, super healthy”, as Kerr, with her doe eyes, smooth forehead and self-seriousness, nodded magnanimously. The acceptance, endorsement and promotion of harmful claims made on Cavallari’s show are everything that’s wrong with podcasting.

Podcasting, unlike more traditional forms of media, is unregulated. Aside from adhering to the defamation, hate speech or copyright laws of the country in which it is made, and the guidelines on the platform (Apple, Spotify, Audible) that hosts it, a podcaster bears no responsibility for what they say or broadcast and will suffer no consequences if what they say or broadcast is untrue or reckless.

Indeed, broadcasting that which is untrue and reckless can be to a podcaster’s benefit: maximising reach, drawing in listeners, developing communities and tribes – it is exactly how podcasts like The Joe Rogan Experience have helped to spread so much misinformation and allowed conspiracy theories to proliferate.

Ridiculous claims like Kerr’s, and those made recently by Steven Bartlett on his Diary of a CEO – about how drinking wine ruined his life for a few days – are extreme, mockable, and usually go viral, but that doesn’t cauterise the risk that some people will absorb them as truth.

The dangers of podcasting aren’t all about what is loudly promoted, but what is quietly accepted. Unlike, say, a reputable journalist, Cavallari has no duty to fact-check or question what someone says on her programme. She may not have the knowledge to. She, and other podcast presenters like her whose shows are an extension of a multi-hyphenate career from a media personality, have platforms as big as some traditional broadcasters, but do not have the same accountability for what they put out.

Podcasting has become an industry that is fuelled by big personalities going unquestioned. For every well-researched news show committed to honesty and reasonable inquiry, there are about 300 more hosted by clueless celebrities without the expertise nor the courage to do anything but pacify their guests and nod along.

Much of the time, it benefits them to. Interview shows, especially, are only sustained by the willingness of guests to appear, which they will be reluctant to do if they expect the conversation to be difficult, inquisitive or in any way obstructive to their own self-promotion. A little inconvenience like “the truth” can get in the way of that.

Some programmes, from Alexandra Cooper’s Call Her Daddy, which featured Kamala Harris in the run up to the 2024 US general election, to How to Fail with Elizabeth Day, which this week featured an interview with Andy Burnham, do recognise their influence and take it seriously. 

However, a far greater number serve as an extension of a personal brand for celebrities who themselves may stand to gain from their guests in future. They want to be liked, to appear on their guest’s own podcast one day, to profit from cross-promotion. It’s a PR exercise that goes round and round – at best sycophantic and at worst dangerous.

Now that podcasting has undergone a video revolution, it’s getting worse. Every show is filmed to allow conversations to be clipped into digestible, context-free, short-form video content, to be distributed on social media and algorithmically parachuted into the feeds of people outside of its active audience – like me, who had never before listened to Cavallari’s show, which ironically enough is titled Let’s Be Honest. Podcasts – and the content and claims within – are now designed to seep into our passive consciousness, where they are normalised without us even realising. That is far more insidious than traditional media. Especially since so many podcasts are hosted by influencers – people whose very job title denotes the impact they have on others.

A BBC newsreader would be held to account for revelling in the return of smoking (as I heard recently on the American podcast It’s Me Tinx), or for promoting spurious health claims like Kerr’s – but their career doesn’t rely on a legion of impressionable people emulating their lifestyle. Anyone, no matter their qualifications, can start a podcast and disseminate whatever ideas they want to on multiple mediums and devices. Surely they require regulation more than anyone, and yet there is no Ofcom to complain to when things are wrong, irresponsible, in poor taste, or dangerous. It is a Wild West.

Podcasting gave everyone a voice. It democratised broadcasting. It changed the meaning of free speech. They are intimate, freeform, unfiltered – it’s what makes them so easy to listen to and what distinguishes them from other media. But as Kerr’s fear of kale and spinach threatens to brainwash me, I’m starting to wonder if a filter is overdue.
news.author: Sarah Carson

news.title: What to expect in Hawaii’s state primary
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — An ongoing corruption scandal involving Hawaii’s lieutenant governor looms over Saturday’s state primary as nine candidates jockey to replace her. Meanwhile, a longtime Democratic congressman who bucked his party and supported one of President Donald Trump’s top legislative priorities faces a tough primary challenge.

Five Democrats and four Republicans are seeking their parties’ nominations to succeed embattled Democratic Hawaii Lt. Gov. Sylvia Luke, who pleaded not guilty in July to bribery charges stemming from her 2022 campaign when she was a state lawmaker.

Hawaii’s lieutenant governorship has long been a steppingstone to higher office in the state. Democratic Gov. Josh Green and Democratic U.S. Sens. Mazie Hirono and Brian Schatz all served as lieutenant governor. The governor and lieutenant governor are elected individually and do not run on the same ticket.

The Democratic field includes Kauai County Mayor Derek Kawakami, state Rep. Della Au Belatti and former state Deputy Attorney General John Choi. Kawakami has led in fundraising. He also has the backing of a political action committee tied to the carpenters union that has spent roughly $2 million on his behalf, according to state campaign finance records.

Republican Daniel Anthony was the top spender among his primary opponents for the first few weeks of July, but at about $6,900, it was a fraction of spending by the leading Democratic candidates. 

Luke has been on an unpaid leave of absence since April. Green named state official Keith Regan as acting lieutenant governor. Regan isn’t running for a full term.

Green is seeking reelection as governor. He faces three Democratic primary challengers. Republicans have a two-way primary.

In the 1st Congressional District, Democratic U.S. Rep. Ed Case seeks a seventh full term but first must overcome four primary challengers, including state Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole.

Keohokalole has criticized Case for crossing party lines in April 2025 to support Trump’s signature election legislation, known as the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, or the SAVE Act. The Republican president’s legislation would, among other things, require voters to prove their U.S. citizenship when registering for federal elections.

Case has said, including in a recent Hawaii Public Radio interview, that the version of the SAVE Act he voted for provided accommodations for voters who don’t present the required documentation, including signing a written attestation of their citizenship. He has voted against subsequent versions of the bill that didn’t provide those accommodations.

Case and Keohokalole were evenly matched in terms of campaign fundraising and spending, although Case had a sizable advantage in terms of cash in the bank heading into the campaign’s final stretch.

The winner will face Republican Adriel Lam, who is unopposed in the primary.

Hawaii’s 1st Congressional District is heavily Democratic. Case won reelection in 2024 with about 72% of the vote. Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris received about 62% of the district vote in the presidential election against Trump.

About half of Hawaii’s 25 state Senate seats and all 51 state House seats are up in 2026. Democrats hold overwhelming majorities in both chambers.

Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied:

When do polls close?

Polls close at 7 p.m. local time, which is 1 a.m. ET Sunday.

What’s on the ballot?

The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare winners in contested primaries for governor, lieutenant governor, U.S. House, state Senate and state House.

Who gets to vote?

Any registered voter in Hawaii may participate in any party’s primary.

How many voters are there?

As of the November 2024 general election, there were about 861,000 registered voters in Hawaii.

How many people actually vote?

About 195,000 voters cast ballots in the 2024 Democratic U.S. Senate primary and about 54,000 in the Republican primary. Turnout was higher in the 2022 primaries for governor. About 251,000 Democratic primary voters and about 76,000 Republican primary voters cast ballots that year.

About 91,000 voters cast ballots in the 1st Congressional District Democratic primary in 2024.

How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot? 

Hawaii conducts its elections primarily by mail. Ballots are mailed to all registered voters. Less than 2% of 2024 state primary voters cast their ballots in person.

As of Tuesday, about 179,000 ballots had already been cast in Saturday’s election.

When are early and absentee votes released?

All four counties in Hawaii tend to release most of their results from early in-person and mail voting in their first vote updates of the night, before any in-person Election Day votes are released. Almost all results are released by the final election night vote update.

How long does vote-counting usually take?

Hawaii typically has three vote updates after polls close: the first at roughly 1:30 a.m. ET, the second at roughly 4:30 a.m. ET, and the third and final in the early hours of the Monday following the election.

In the 2024 state primary, the AP first reported results at 1:22 a.m. ET, or 22 minutes after polls closed. The last vote update of the night was at 4:48 a.m. ET, with about 92% of total votes counted.

In the 2022 state primary, the first results were available at 1:58 a.m. ET, and the last election night update was at 4:45 a.m. ET, with about 86% of total votes counted.

When will the AP declare a winner?

The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.

How do recounts work?

Recounts in Hawaii are automatic if the vote margin is 100 votes or less, or 0.25% of the total votes cast for a contest, whichever is smaller. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.

Are we there yet?

As of Saturday, there will be 87 days until the 2026 midterm elections.

Follow the AP’s coverage of the 2026 election at https://apnews.com/projects/elections-2026/.

news.title: Oh, C'mon, Jill, You Don't Actually Believe That About Kamala Harris
news.text:
Host Kelly Ripa asked Biden on her SiriusXM podcast “Let’s Talk Off Camera” whether she believed there would be a woman president in her lifetime. While Biden said she expected former Vice President Kamala Harris to win the 2024 election, she conceded that she no longer believes she will see a woman in the White House.

“I have a sort of a final question, and I fear the answer. I really do. I fear the answer,” Ripa said. “Do you think we’ll ever see a woman president in our lifetimes?”

Biden, 75, pointed to her age as a reason why she wouldn’t see a woman become president.

“In my lifetime, well, I’m 75, so you know I feel like probably not in my lifetime,” Biden said. “Kelly, but maybe in yours.”

Ripa asked Biden again whether she really believed that.

“I mean, you and I believe in a woman president. I mean, it’s like no question, right? No question,” Biden said. “But I really did think last time that Kamala was going to win. I mean, I was out on the campaign trail for her. I saw the excitement. I saw the crowds. I saw at the convention. I mean, I saw all the energy, and I thought finally we’re going to have a woman president.”

She said that she was stunned the morning after Election Day when she learned Harris had lost.

“I must tell you, I was shocked the morning after when I got up at 5o’clock in the morning to feed Willow and get ready for the day, and I found out that she had lost,” Biden said. “I mean, shocked.”

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed Wasn’t the Only One Who Won on Tuesday. Democrats and Republicans Alike Are Furious.
news.text:
Come back with me to the autumn of 2021. I’m a writer who has been sent out on assignment to the stucco estates of suburban Los Angeles to profile a young socialist named Hasan Piker. Piker initially came to fame a few years prior while making YouTube videos for his uncle’s media company The Young Turks. After leaving, he built a brand as a Bernie-boosting leftist pundit, his rapid-fire takes meted out through the livestreaming platform Twitch. Thousands of young people were tuning in to Piker’s daily eight-hour broadcasts; they watched him scroll through New York Times headlines and riff on cable-news segments, all filtered through his chagrin for bland liberal consensus. I plopped down on a couch across from Piker, his body partially obscured by a towering PlayStation 5, and asked what he made of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar, who were then just beginning to make a name for themselves in Democratic politics. Did Piker sense that the party was changing?

“We’re ants, we’re nothing,” I remember him saying, sizing up the state of the American left. Looking back, he was right. The Sanders movement was quashed by Joe Biden, of all people. At that moment, the moderate flank seemed to be keeping people like Piker in check.

Now come back with me to Tuesday evening, when the Democratic Socialists of America–endorsed public health official Abdul El-Sayed triumphed over establishment candidate Haley Stevens in a fiercely contested primary for Michigan’s Democratic Senate nomination. When I visited Piker’s Twitch profile on election night, I wasn’t surprised to find him broadcasting live from El-Sayed’s reception. Piker had rallied with the candidate throughout the campaign. Back in 2025, El-Sayed had outlined on Piker’s stream his platform of economic populism and an end to military aid to Israel, and Piker had early on joined El-Sayed on the campaign trail, notably leading the streamer’s past comments about 9/11 and Israel to become a major issue in the race. Despite the heat, El-Sayed refused to disavow Piker.

And when El-Sayed won his primary, there Piker was, looking on from the crowd. Compared to the 30-year-old I interviewed five years ago, Piker looked considerably more grown-up. Instead of the ratty, paint-spattered graphic tee he had worn that afternoon, he was smartly attired in a loose-fitting linen suit and tie, a Palestinian flag pinned to its left lapel. This was supposed to be a coronation—some polls had El-Sayed up as much as 15 points—but his margin of victory, less than 1 point, raised some questions about the DSA’s vulnerabilities in November.

He may have looked more polished, but he had the same energy that he used to deploy hour after hour on Twitch. Piker immediately went on the offensive. He stared directly into the camera and offered this summation of the campaign ahead: “Everyone being like, ‘Abdul has a fuck-ton of work to do mending bridges,’ … you are all unbelievably Islamophobic pieces of shit,” he said. “You literally called the dude a fucking terrorist for months on end, and called him a sexist, misogynist, terrorist, bad candidate. … And now you’re going to say, sit there and be like, ‘You really got to come to me now.’ What are you talking about? Do you want to win or not? Lock the fuck in.”

In other words, Piker was still Piker. And on Tuesday night, it was clear he will be one of the Democratic Party’s main characters going into the 2028 election cycle, for better or worse—for both the party and Piker himself.

It’s not just El-Sayed who is cozying up to Piker. The streamer has already claimed a number of coups this cycle, having pushed for New York’s Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier and Colorado’s Melat Kiros, three DSA-aligned candidates who beat more-mainstream Democrats and are now shoo-ins for the House of Representatives next year. He has boosted Wisconsin’s socialist gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong, who still looks strong in her race, sometimes despite herself. If El-Sayed makes it to Capitol Hill, the win will represent, by far, Piker’s most impressive bounty yet.

Which is why this week Politico asked Piker if he thought of himself as a kingmaker. Piker demurred, but I wasn’t surprised by the line of questioning. The man has achieved significant political capital without moderating anything he stands for. The right—perhaps invigorated by Stevens’ strong showing—perceives this as a weakness. In the months ahead, Republicans will be running against Piker just as much as they’re running against the Democratic Party. In fact, it has already started. Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee in the upcoming Michigan Senate race, just released his first digital attack ad against El-Sayed. The first images feature El-Sayed and Piker at a campaign stop together. “You are who your friends are,” reads the text at the bottom of the screen.

You are likely already familiar with Piker’s controversies. They are the same ones Rogers focuses on in that video, and they’re repeated, ad nauseam, every time Piker appears on television. To quickly recap: In 2019 the streamer said that America “deserved” 9/11, a comment he apologized for shortly afterward and has since disavowed. His staunch pro-Palestinian advocacy has also landed him in reedy territory; he has said he doesn’t have “an issue” with Hezbollah, and he once interviewed a Houthi militant on his Twitch stream. (The two talked about, among other things, the anime series One Piece.) Republicans were looking for a bogeyman to epitomize perceived DSA fanaticism, and they found their guy. As Piker’s profile has risen, so has his presence on Fox News. On Wednesday, Stephen Miller appeared on Hannity to lambast Piker, in his characteristically florid way, as “heinous, deplorable, and monstrous,” chastising El-Sayed for associating himself with “that kind of evil.” This opinion is echoed by the moderate flank of the liberal elite. James Carville, for example, passed through Fox News recently too. “I’m not going to be in the same party as Hasan Piker,” he said. “If he becomes a force in the Democratic Party, I’m out of here.”

None of this should be surprising. After a brief honeymoon period, Piker was always going to find himself at odds with the establishment. Looking back, he gained a foothold in mainstream politics only because of the humiliating defeat of Kamala Harris, and the soul-searching that followed. Democrats, the thinking went, needed to find a “liberal Joe Rogan”—someone with the right kind of politics and an audience of those downwardly mobile young men the party was hemorrhaging. Instead, they found Piker, an ideologue who was never going to betray his heart. The two sides played nice in the heady days of 2025, when the midterms were far enough off in the distance and everyone was willing to pay lip service to Piker’s more exotic ideas. He appeared on Crooked Media and NPR and sat for Q&As with Ross Douthat, outlining his worldview for skeptical but receptive hosts. Inevitably, though, order would be enforced, and Piker would once again be painted as the enemy. Because Carville is right. Piker’s beliefs are incompatible with the sclerotic principles of American liberalism. Unfortunately for Carville and his ilk, that’s exactly why so many young progressives were tuning in to his stream in the first place.

It’s worth noting that nobody—not Republicans, not Democrats, not anyone on the fringes—can determine for certain the weight a Piker endorsement carries. A poll conducted in April found that 13 percent of Michigan voters have a favorable view of Piker, 7 percent hold an unfavorable view of him, and a whopping 80 percent “haven’t heard enough to say.” But his outsize influence on intraparty strife seems clear already and is certain only to grow in the months ahead. Perhaps the Rogers campaign is correct, and El-Sayed’s connection to the Twitch streamer will prove to be uniquely toxic, torpedoing his chances in the general. Or maybe Piker’s vision of a dramatically reimagined Democratic Party will catch fire, cracking open wild possibilities for the future. That, I think, is what elites on both sides of the aisle are especially afraid of.

But come back with me one more time, to the night before Donald Trump was inaugurated for his second term as president. I was profiling Piker for the second time in my life, right as his influence was beginning to crest and the Democratic brand was approaching an unfathomable low. I asked him about the opportunity at hand. Could he envision a future where he was a major player in the party? “I’m not changing. That’s the thing. I have a real political opinion, a real way I see the world,” he told me. “If a day comes where I’m side by side with the Democratic Party, that means the Democratic Party has changed its ways.”

We’ll find out how much the Democratic Party has changed soon enough. For now, this is Piker’s moment. Democrats and Republicans alike ought to brace for impact.
news.summary: We’re about to find out what he really means for the left.

news.title: GOP plans to fend off latest Democrat promise for new long-term care benefit
news.text:
Bobby Jindal, former GOP governor of Louisiana and health policy expert, told the Washington Examiner that lawmakers should focus on developing workable strategies to address an aging population instead of creating a new entitlement program for long-term elder care.

“Of course the Democrat response is going to simply be let’s just add new benefits and not worry about how to pay for them,” Jindal said. “I think a more thoughtful approach would be to re-examine what should be a Medicaid responsibility, what should be a Medicare responsibility, what should be your private sector responsibility, and what is possible with new technologies.”

Jindal, who now serves as chair of the Healthy America program at the Trump-aligned America First Policy Institute, said it is too early to definitively say what the Republican platform on the problem will look like in the 2028 election, but he says he sees it as a critical issue in the coming years.

By 2030, all 73 million baby boomers will be 65, a trend demographers at the Census Bureau refer to as a “gray tsunami.” The Alzheimer’s Association estimates that nearly 7 in 10 people turning 65 will need long-term care at the end of their lives due to dementia-related diseases.

According to the long-term care services resource company CareScout, the annual cost for an in-home health aide was roughly $78,000 annually in 2024. A private room in a skilled nursing home facility was on average $128,000 per year. 

The division between Medicare and Medicaid, the joint federal-state insurance program for low-income people, creates a complicated and fragmented system for paying for long-term care, with most costs for home health or nursing facilities being covered directly by patients and their families.

Medicare only covers short-term, limited residential care and a limited amount of skilled at-home nursing care. Medicaid, by contrast, covers the majority of long-term residential home-based care for people below a certain income threshold. 

Brian Blase, president of the free-market Paragon Health Institute, told the Washington Examiner coming up with a policy solution for long-term care benefits is going to be even more important not only as baby boomers age but also as families have fewer children.

“I think the role of the family is appropriate to take care of your elder relatives,” Blase said. “It’s an important family responsibility [but to] the extent that families are smaller, that does add pressure to the public sector.”

New benefit but old playbook from Democrats

Democrats have long sought a new home health and long-term care benefits program.

In 2010, Democrats enacted, as part of Obamacare, the Community Living Assistance Services and Supports, or CLASS, Act with the intention of creating a national, voluntary long-term services insurance program financed by individual premium contributions. But by 2013, the program was abandoned because it was not fiscally sustainable and was repealed.

Former President Joe Biden pledged to include $400 billion for in-home and community-based services, or HCBS, as part of the 2021 Build Back Better bill. But the funding was eventually cut from the Senate-passed version of the bill.

On the 2024 campaign trail, then-Vice President Kamala Harris also pitched to the public to add at-home long-term care benefits to Medicare, appealing to the so-called sandwich generation that takes care of both young children and elderly parents.

Wyden’s call to Democrats this summer, in the form of a Dear Colleague letter, was more of a request to brainstorm a home health Medicare benefit than a concrete policy proposal. Staff for the Senate Finance Committee, of which Wyden is the leading Democrat, told reporters at the time that the goal of the letter was mainly to spark dialogue among senators rather than committing to a specific dollar figure for any new benefits. 

But the projected cost of any new benefit would be critical, considering the financial strain Medicare is already under.

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimated earlier this year that Medicare spending is projected to double over the next decade, reaching $2 trillion and accounting for 4% of projected gross domestic product by 2036.

Last year, the Medicare Trustees projected the trust fund for Medicare Part A would be insolvent by 2033, three years earlier than previously projected.

Blase said that any new Medicare benefit ought to be at net-zero cost to the budget.

“Congress needs to, if they’re going to add a new benefit, there needs to be some trade-off because the program is on a totally unsustainable financial trajectory,” he said.

GOP solution: Tackling abuse and fraud

Conservative policy advisers see the fix to the problems of long-term care policy as an extension of the GOP’s broader goal of targeting waste, fraud, and abuse in federal entitlement programs. 

Blase said one of the primary ways to improve the state of long-term care would be to tighten eligibility requirements for Medicaid coverage of home health and nursing home care, which would in turn create an opportunity for a more robust long-term care insurance market to fill the void.

Medicaid rules require that recipients “spend down” the majority of their assets and have a limited take-home income in order to qualify for long-term care coverage.

But Medicaid planners and elder law attorneys frequently advise clients on how to avoid losing their nest eggs before obtaining Medicaid to cover long-term care costs through legal loopholes. Through financial maneuvers such as irrevocable trusts and spousal asset transfers, wealthy individuals and families can often access Medicaid benefits to pay for long-term care.

“Our main recommendation is to limit Medicaid to the truly poor with limited assets, and that people need to, if they have assets, put them towards their long-term care expenses rather than relying on the government,” Blase said. 

Along similar lines, Jindal and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich co-authored an opinion piece in Fox News Digital last month arguing that identifying fraudulent billing by providers is essential to building on the home health and long-term care programs already funded by taxpayer dollars. 

The White House Fraud Task Force, led by Vice President JD Vance, has reportedly identified nearly $230 billion in fraud and abuse since March. Much of this fraud has been through improper billing of high-risk services such as community-based care and home care for seniors and people with disabilities, as well as hospice centers. 

In addition to using artificial intelligence to identify billing irregularities, Jindal said, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services could, in theory, leverage new technologies to verify home health companies are sending aides to real patients in a way that does not jeopardize legitimate providers.

“Whether through a smartphone type device, or GPS device, there are devices, there are technologies that can help to automate some of this compliance,” Jindal said.

Jindal said program integrity measures, rather than just creating a new benefits program, are “about protecting vulnerable seniors who deserve high-quality services provided by honest providers.”

news.title: Trump-backed incumbent loses primary after super PAC bankrolled by Dems meddled in race
news.text: Rep. Andy Ogles, R-Tenn., was defeated in a primary challenge on Thursday evening by Republican challenger Charlie Hatcher, a farmer and the state's former commissioner of agriculture. Although the primary was far from a top-watched contest coming into the 2026 primaries, it served as a microcosm of larger forces at play in the Republican Party. From a break in endorsements between President Donald Trump and Tennessee’s Republican Governor Bill Lee to millions being pumped into the district over environmental policy, the race attracted attention well beyond its borders. The Invest in Tomorrow Coalition super PAC had spent roughly $2 million opposing Ogles and supporting Hatcher. The group has raised $6.7 million this year, making Ogles a sizable portion of their spending this cycle. TOP TRUMP ALLY WARNS SUPER PAC BANKROLLED BY DEM BILLIONAIRE IS MEDDLING IN GOP PRIMARY The way that Ogles sees it, it’s an attempt to show Republicans what happens when lawmakers attempt to claw back government funding for renewable energy sources. Like many other Republicans, Ogles has called to scale back renewable energy investments made under the Biden Administration. "When you have a group spending roughly $2 million in a Republican primary, that tells you how much money they're making off of government subsidies, and they're upset that the government welfare has been taken away from them," Ogles told Fox News Digital in an interview. A Fox News Digital review of FEC filings discovered that the super PAC is bankrolled by Chris Larsen, the California-based billionaire chairman of Ripple, a financial technology company that, according to its website, offers crypto solutions for businesses. Larsen is also a frequent Democratic donor, having contributed $5,444,975 to support Kamala Harris's failed presidential campaign. More than just his opposition to government-backed renewable energy initiatives, Ogles thinks it’s his proximity to Trump that has made him a target. "It's because I'm close to the president. It is because I am outspoken. And quite frankly, it is because I speak plainly on these issues," Ogles said. GOP GOVERNOR ENDORSES CANDIDATE CHALLENGING TRUMP-BACKED CONGRESSMAN IN REPUBLICAN US HOUSE PRIMARY For his own part, Hatcher, a fifth-generation Tennessee dairy farmer, has pitched himself as someone unencumbered by the political scene and ensnaring interests. "I think there’s something missing in Washington. There’s a lack of farmer common sense. There’s a lack of work ethic. One of my strengths is problem-solving, looking for solutions, looking for collaborations and supporting the Trump Administration and Speaker Johnson on their agenda," Hatcher said in a campaign video. Notably, Tennessee’s Republican governor put his weight behind Hatcher late on Tuesday evening, citing a personal relationship between them. "He served as my commissioner of agriculture; I know Charlie. I know his conservative values and how much he loves our country. Charlie has stood with President Trump since day one," Lee said in a video. Trump, who has endorsed Ogles, reaffirmed his support for the conservative firebrand ahead of the primary. "Andy will be really enshrined as one of the best congressmen that you’ll ever see. He’s just fantastic," Trump said. "Andy has always been there when we needed him and when I needed him. He’s been a great help. He’s been a source of inspiration to a lot of people in Congress," Trump said in a post to Truth Social earlier this year. TENNESSEE PASSES NEW CONGRESSIONAL MAP LIKELY TO FLIP FINAL DEM SEAT AS PROTESTS ERUPT INSIDE CAPITOL CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Having captured the Republican nomination, Hatcher now advances to a general election he’s heavily favored to win on Nov. 3. He won re-election in 2024 in a 56.9% to 39.5% victory over Maryam Abolfazli.
news.summary: A super PAC bankrolled by a California billionaire and frequent Democratic donor spent $2 million to unseat Andy Ogles over renewable energy policy.

news.title: US Sen. Marsha Blackburn wins GOP nomination for Tennessee governor
news.text:
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn won Tennessee's Republican nomination for governor on Aug. 6, defeating two other conservative candidates and cementing her status as the heavy favorite to become the first woman to lead the state, NBC News and the Associated Press have projected.

"One year ago, we set out on this journey with one goal: to make Tennessee America's conservative leader and show the nation what strong, bold, conservative leadership looks like." Blackburn posted on X shortly before 9:30 pm ET. "Tonight, I am humbled and honored that you've chosen me as your Republican nominee for Governor."

In November's midterm, Blackburn will face Jerri Green, who won the Democratic nomination, CNN and the Associated Press projected.

But it will be a massive uphill battle for Green, a Memphis council member. A Democrat has not sat in the state's governor seat since former Gov. Phil Bredesen was termed out in 2011 after his 2006 victory, and Republican candidates have dominated the state in recent years. 

Blackburn, 74, entered the Republican primary race the clear favorite over U.S. Rep. John Rose and state Rep. Monty Fritts, at one point holding double-digital leads in early polling. She is popular among Republicans and was the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate from Tennessee, currently serving her second Senate term after four terms in the U.S. House of Representatives.

President Donald Trump did not endorse a candidate for the Republican primary, although Blackburn and Rose are both strong supporters of the president. Trump swept the state in 2024 with an almost 30-point-lead over Kamala Harris.

Blackburn's goal is "to make Tennessee America’s conservative leader," according to her campaign Twitter, and her campaign spotlights her commitment to Trump, his "America First Agenda" and the Make America Great Again movement.

On the issues, her campaign advocated for core-Republican platforms such as economic growth through tax cuts, fighting crime and illegal immigration, cutting wasteful government spending, parental rights and removing "woke" curriculums from schools.

"She fights every day for President Donald Trump’s America First agenda, to keep men out of girls’ sports, hold big tech accountable, defend life, protect American farmland from Communist China, secure our borders, and deport all illegal aliens," Blackburn's website says.

Blackburn's campaign also gained national attention when she released a July campaign video where the senator sat in a Chinese food restaurant crumbling Fortune cookies to show "how hard am I going to crack down on China." She also faced criticism for not debating her two primary opponents.

The race tightened as the primary neared but Blackburn stayed in the lead until her final victory.

Rose's campaign contrasted Blackburn's, pointing to his family roots as an eighth-generation farmer in the state and highlighting that he is "not a career politician." Similar to Blackburn, though, he relied on a connection to Trump, calling himself an "unapologetic supporter" of the president who will align with Trump's "blueprint." He focused on five campaign priorities – education, infrastructure, healthcare, energy and economic and community development.

Fritts ran a small-government "liberty & less government" campaign that called for 10 pillars including eliminating a grocery sales tax, defending the Second Amendment, supporting voter ID laws and removing incentives that attracted "illegal aliens" to the state.

On the Democratic side, two candidates besides Green – Carnita Atwater and Tim Cyr – were on the primary ballot. Green campaigned on supporting working families, strengthening public schools, expanding Medicaid in rural parts of the state, "common-sense" gun laws and clean climate preservation.

This is a developing story.

news.title: AZ Democrat Katie Hobbs Still Could Do the Lamest Thing Ever Ahead of Friday Deadline in Gov's Race
news.text:
A crucial deadline in the hotly-contested 2026 Arizona governor's race is just hours away on Friday. That means Governor Katie Hobbs (D-AZ) still has time to screw up her pick for lieutenant governor.

Earlier this week, legacy media lapdogs The New York Times did her reelection campaign a favor with this scoop floating the possibility that a "longtime Republican" mayor might become her running mate.

The piece claims that sources close to both Giles and Hobbs told The NYT that he was the pick.

The official deadline on gubernatorial running mates is 60 days before the November election, but the AZ Secretary of State's office told both Republican nominee Rep. Andy Biggs' (AZ-05) and Hobbs' campaign that the running mate's name needed to be submitted before Friday, Aug. 7 to give them time to print the general election ballots.

As I wrote about a week ago, Biggs announced that his running mate is Sine Kerr, a pro-life conservative champion, dairy farmer, and former Arizona state senator. 

Read More: Historic: Meet the First Ever Lieutenant Governor Nom for AZ - She's Appealing to Rural Voters

The clock is ticking still for Gov. Hobbs to announce her lieutenant governor nod, though, and on Thursday, someone's finally stating the obvious: if she does pick Giles, it does not magically make her bipartisan. 

The Republican Party of Arizona's Chairman Sergio Arellano put out a statement which began by exposing Mayor Giles' longtime kabuki theater for what it is:

To be clear, this political theater needs to stop.John Giles may no longer call himself a Republican, but his actions have aligned him with Democrats for years. On May 17, 2026, after nearly forty years as a registered Republican, he left the Republican Party, registered as No Party Preference, and pulled a Democratic primary ballot. That is a matter of public record.

Long before changing his voter registration, Giles had already made his choice. He endorsed Kamala Harris for President, spoke at the Democratic National Convention, endorsed Katie Hobbs, and repeatedly attacked the Republican Party and the conservative movement that helped elect him.John Giles didn't suddenly change when he changed his voter registration. His paperwork simply caught up with the political choices he'd been making for years.

His statement continued with the larger problem Hobbs has: being honest with voters:

"It is not surprising that Governor Hobbs is trying to pull a fast one on Arizona voters by pretending to act in a bipartisan fashion. Frankly, it’s her only hope. Unfortunately for her, Arizona voters are smarter than that. They know the difference between genuine bipartisanship and political theater, and they won’t be fooled by a last-minute rebranding campaign."Truth be told, I still don’t believe John Giles will ultimately be her choice. Given his lack of political accomplishments and his phony Republican credentials, I wouldn’t be surprised if Governor Hobbs eventually turns to Chief of Staff Chad Campbell instead. That decision might make a handful of her deep-pocketed political cronies very happy, but it would also expose this entire bipartisan charade for exactly what it is—a political marketing campaign, not a governing philosophy. Frankly, Hobbs choosing Campbell would make my job even easier...."Governor Hobbs can change running mates. She can’t change her record. Arizona voters haven’t forgotten the vetoes, the failed priorities, or the direction this state has taken over the last four years. We look forward to defeating Governor Hobbs—Arizona’s ‘Veto Queen’—and whoever ultimately joins her ticket this November."

In case you missed my previous writing on Hobbs, the title is not an exaggeration; Governor Janet Napolitano (D-AZ) had what seemed like a forever record on vetoes, with local progressive rag The Phoenix New Times proudly cheering her vetoes of "181 bills from 2003-09." During Hobbs' first two years in office, she wielded the veto pen 216 times.

Read More: Arizona's Gov. Hobbs Seeks to Rally Progressive Dems With Post-Primary Slur on GOP 'White Supremacists'

In 2026, that veto tally for the uber-partisan Hobbs? 151.

No one who lives here in the Copper State is fooled by John Giles' boasting about being a "longtime Republican." It's a convenient label he slaps on to try to stay in the good graces of the media. If someone had a news camera, he was in front of it during the 2024 presidential cycle. Indeed, less than two weeks after Vice President Kamala Harris launched her run for president, Giles signed on as an early endorsee.

Anyway, Hobbs could do the lamest thing ever in the next few hours — which is totally on brand for her.

news.title: Guest Opinion: Once again, national Democrats are making a primary mistake
news.text:
It is clear in hindsight, and was clear to many at the time, that the choice to sideline New Hampshire in the 2024 Democratic presidential primary process was designed to spare President Joe Biden from scrutiny over his ability to mount a vigorous reelection campaign. South Carolina was chosen to go first.

As New Hampshire, following state law, held its primary first anyway, there was a farcical super-PAC effort by Biden surrogates to win the write-in vote here without Biden campaigning. As that succeeded, the New Hampshire delegates were seated at the Democratic convention.

Now it seems clear that New Hampshire will be passed over again by Democrats, based on the premise that it is not diverse enough, in favor of South Carolina or Nevada. The former would be a very strange proving ground. Biden got only 43.4 percent of the South Carolina vote in 2020, even as he went on to win nationally. There is just one Democrat in the state’s seven-member House delegation. The state legislature has been Republican since 1998.

Nevada is also a peculiar political ecosystem. It was there that President Donald Trump, as a candidate, unveiled his June 2024 “no tax on tips” proposal, which Kamala Harris parroted at a Nevada rally two months later, and that led to a four-year suspension of taxes on tips in the federal budget reconciliation bill that passed last year.

If Nevada goes first, a successful Democratic candidate will have to appeal to the critical bloc of Culinary Workers Union members, which could shape his or her remaining campaign in ways that may not appeal to the broader nation. It reminds me of the ethanol pledge that “The West Wing” so well depicted presidential candidates Arnold Vinick and Matt Santos struggling with at a Corn Growers Expo in Iowa.

There is no such organized group to pander to in New Hampshire. And yet, for those who might suggest our state lacks the diversity to go first, I would ask what one’s definition of diversity is. Isn’t age a demographic? New Hampshire has the nation’s second-oldest population. Nationally, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, “From 2020 to 2024, the older population grew by 13.0 percent, significantly outpacing the 1.4 percent growth of working-age adults (ages 18 to 64), while the number of children declined by 1.7 percent.”

By 2034, U.S. sales of adult diapers are projected to exceed baby diaper sales. Our aging population is going to place a strain on safety net programs like Medicaid and Medicare, and New Hampshire would be a great place to hone a message to senior voters. After all, according to the trustees of the Medicare Hospital Insurance trust fund, it will be insolvent by 2033. Kind of a big deal.

There are an estimated 4 million tipped workers in the country. In contrast, in 2024 data showed that 43.3 million U.S. citizens who are 65-and-older voted, easily the biggest age demographic to vote. It might be somewhat important for a Democratic candidate to win over these older voters, given that Trump won them 51-47 percent over Harris.

Treating New Hampshire as flyover country would also be taking for granted a state where Republicans have a lock on state government and the presidential vote isn’t a given. Had Al Gore won New Hampshire in 2000, Florida would have been immaterial. Although Hillary Clinton lost the electoral college in 2016, she nearly lost New Hampshire too — carrying it by only a 47.6 percent-47.2 percent margin over Trump.

Finally, the retail politics required to win the New Hampshire primary, instead of just pouring money into a major media market like Las Vegas, has made for more nimble candidates in both political parties. It would be a shame for national Democrats to devalue that tradition. And it would be a big loss to the civic experience of Granite Staters.

news.title: ‘Uncommitted’ founder Alawieh who pushed Democrats to vote against Biden over Gaza wins primary
news.text: Abbas Alawieh, a founder of the Uncommitted movement that pressured former US president Joe Biden to change his Israel policy, is the projected winner of a Democratic primary for Michigan's state Senate. Alawieh rose to national prominence as a key architect of the campaign to withhold votes from Biden during Michigan's presidential primary in 2024, a protest against the administration's support for Israel as it inflicted mounting casualties in Gaza. Alawieh defeated state representative Erin Byrnes in Tuesday's primary to represent Michigan's 2nd Senate District, a heavily Arab-American area covering Dearborn and parts of Detroit - and the epicenter of the Uncommitted effort. He won 59% of the vote to Byrnes' 41% after more than 95% of votes were counted, according to the Associated Press, and is now almost certain to win the solid-blue state Senate seat in November. Alawieh, who was born in Lebanon and grew up in Dearborn, acknowledged his victory without giving a speech on Wednesday. His staff announced that Alawieh's maternal grandfather, Hajj Kassem Bazzi, died Tuesday night as they awaited the election results. “Please keep Abbas's family in your prayers as they take needed time together,” Alawieh's team said in a statement. “Abbas will share his own thoughts on the race soon. For now, thank you to every community that made this win possible.”Alawieh was backed by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. He previously worked as a staffer for congressional Democrats, including Michigan Rep. Rashida Tlaib, former Michigan Rep. Andy Levin, and former Missouri rep. Cori Bush, who lost a primary against Rep. Wesley Bell on Tuesday. Over 100,000 vote for 'uncommitted' in 2024 Democratic primaryAlawieh, alongside Layla Elabed, co-founded the campaign urging Michigan Democrats to vote “uncommitted” in the 2024 Democratic presidential primary. The movement attracted a groundswell of support, including from some Jews, and won more than 100,000 votes, or 13% of the overall vote. Biden was beaten by the uncommitted vote in Dearborn, where Arab Americans make up more than half the population.The Uncommitted movement also spread to other states, rallying more than 650,000 voters nationwide, and crystallized a lack of enthusiasm for Biden, who eventually stepped off the presidential ticket.Alawieh served as one of the Uncommitted delegates at the 2024 Democratic National Convention, where he and other delegates unsuccessfully lobbied to place a Palestinian speaker on the agenda. Alawieh did not make Israel and Gaza a central part of his campaign for the state Senate seat, instead focusing on supporting working families and investing in healthcare, housing, public transit, and education. Still, he told the Michigan Advance in February that his role in the Uncommitted movement resonated with people in his district. “For the people in real life - not on Twitter - it is clear to them that parties' focus on prioritizing funding for war crimes was out of touch with what voters wanted,” he said. “The party was undoubtedly wrong about Gaza in 2024.” Kamala Harris mends fences with Abbas AlawiehWhile some Democrats blamed the Uncommitted campaign for contributing to US President Donald Trump's defeat of former vice president Kamala Harris, who lost Michigan in her 2024 presidential run, Alawieh and Harris have mended fences enough to recently sit down for a meeting.Harris “initiated” the meeting after months of phone calls, Alawieh said in July. “I urge VP Harris and all of our party's leaders to side with peace-loving Americans against endless wars, in opposition to the Israeli military's genocide in Gaza, and against the ethnic cleansing campaign in Lebanon,” he said. Alawieh has said that he voted for Harris against Trump in the 2024 general election, while Elabed did not.The centrality of Israel in Michigan's primaries has spawned bitter divides between Jewish Democrats and others in the party concerning the threat of antisemitism. In one incident that shook Detroit-area Jews earlier this year, Temple Israel in the suburb of West Bloomfield was rammed by a truck laden with explosives. The man who drove the truck, a US citizen from Lebanon, had recently lost several family members in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon. Alawieh responded to the attack by declaring his support for Jewish Michiganders.“We must stand in unequivocal defense of the humanity and safety of our Jewish siblings and denounce this heinous act,” he said in a statement. “My family and I are praying for safety for communities across our state who are feeling afraid right now, and we are holding our Jewish community members extra close.”

news.title: At the Races: Crossing lines
news.text:
Welcome to At the Races! Each week we bring you news and analysis from the CQ Roll Call campaign team. Know someone who’d like to get this newsletter? They can subscribe here.

By Daniela Altimari and Mary Ellen McIntire

Poll after poll suggests Americans are deeply split along partisan lines on most key issues. Signs of that abound, whether in the halls of Congress or on the midterm campaign trail. 

Yet this week brought glimmers of hope for those who believe that finding common ground across rigid political boundaries is healthy for democracy.

In Arizona, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs plans to select a former Republican mayor as her running mate, The New York Times reported. 

Hobbs, a vulnerable purple-state incumbent vying for a second term against Republican Rep. Andy Biggs, is expected to pick John Giles, who was mayor of the Phoenix suburb of Mesa, and recently switched his party registration to “no party preference,’’ the Times reports. Giles has a history of bucking his now-former party; in 2024, he backed Democrats Kamala Harris for president and Ruben Gallego for Senate.

Meanwhile, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, a Democrat running for a second term in another pivotal battleground state, picked up the backing this week of two Republican mayors from South Georgia and a prominent Arizona Republican: former Sen. Jeff Flake.

“I’m still a conservative Republican,’’ Flake told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution. “But character matters. And I want someone in that seat who takes the institution seriously and will protect the institution.”

In Texas, former Tarrant County Judge Glen Whitley, a Republican, endorsed Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico. Whitley had previously announced his opposition to Talarico’s GOP opponent, state Attorney General Ken Paxton. 

“Ken Paxton has spent years embarrassing Texas. He’s known for scandal, indictment, infidelity and putting his own interests ahead of Texans,’’ Whitley said in a radio ad that aired in June.

There haven’t been as many prominent defections among Democrats, but last month, Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo picked up the support of 130 Democrats who are helping to burnish his moderate credentials as he seeks a second term. 

President Donald Trump himself has a history of forging political partnerships with prominent erstwhile Democrats, including former Hawaii Rep. Tulsi Gabbard and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a scion of one of the most celebrated families in Democratic politics.

Bipartisan goodwill, though, only gets you so far. Former Georgia Republican Lt. Gov. Geoff Duncan drew praise from Democrats for backing Harris in 2024. But when he tried to run for governor as a Democrat this year, he couldn’t break even 10 percent of the vote.

Starting gate

Election night recap: Abdul El-Sayed clinched the Democratic Senate nomination in Michigan, narrowly defeating Rep. Haley Stevens in a divisive primary that the party is trying to move on from. Republicans have already begun attacking their newly minted opponent as sympathetic to terrorists and “dangerous” for the swing state. Meanwhile, Missouri Rep. Wesley Bell defeated a comeback attempt from former Rep. Cori Bush, handing progressives a loss on an otherwise mostly good night for Democrats’ left flank. And over the weekend, Del. Stacey Plaskett claimed the Democratic nod for governor of the U.S. Virgin Islands, while Guam Del. James C. Moylan survived a Republican primary challenge, our colleague Nick Eskow reported.

Edwards out: Embattled Rep. Chuck Edwards announced he was ending his reelection bid after the House Ethics Committee recommended the North Carolina Republican be censured for engaging in “persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct” toward two female staffers. Edwards said he’ll serve out the remainder of his term.

Keeping their distance: House Republicans are keeping their distance from their Ohio colleague Max Miller, who is facing allegations of domestic abuse, Roll Call’s Nina Heller reports. Meanwhile, the House Ethics Committee announced it would investigate allegations of domestic violence and abuse and illegal drug use against Miller after he publicly called for the panel to look into him, saying he had “absolutely nothing to hide.”

Redistricting restart: Maryland voters will vote on a constitutional amendment this November that, if approved, would clear the way for Democratic legislators to redraw the state’s congressional map. New lines would almost certainly target Rep. Andy Harris, Maryland’s only Republican in Congress. 

DCCC expands the map again: In a move that reflects their growing confidence ahead of the midterms, House Democrats are zeroing in on 12 additional GOP targets in deep-red districts, nearly all of which Trump carried by double digits in 2024. The new targets include the North Carolina district of NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson. The NRCC dismissed the announcement, saying Democrats were entering "the hallucination phase of the election cycle.” 

Dakota departure: The Democratic Senate nominee in South Dakota ended his campaign following calls from party activists to exit the race and leave independent Brian Bengs as the main competitor against Republican Sen. Mike Rounds. Julian Beaudion’s decision follows similar recent moves by Democrats in deep-red Nebraska and Idaho. 

RIP: Former House Appropriations Chairwoman Kay Granger, the first Republican woman to lead the powerful spending committee, drew bipartisan praise following her death Sunday at 83, our colleague Aidan Quigley reported. The Texan became chairwoman of the Appropriations panel after Republicans won the House during the 2022 midterms. She stepped down in 2024, a year when she was largely absent from Congress as her family reported she was suffering from dementia.

Guv roundup: Gubernatorial matchups were set in two key states that held primaries Tuesday. In battleground Michigan, Republican Rep. John James will take on Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson in the race to succeed term-limited Democrat Gretchen Whitmer. In Kansas, Republican hopes of flipping the governorship rest with state Senate President Ty Masterson, who will face Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher. Meanwhile, in Mississippi, Attorney General Lynn Fitch is hoping to become the Magnolia State’s first female governor, launching her 2027 campaign this week. 

#TN05: Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee endorsed Charlie Hatcher, the former state agriculture commissioner who is challenging GOP Rep. Andy Ogles, in Thursday’s primary. Hatcher also has the backing of Lee’s predecessor, Bill Haslam, though Ogles has the all-important Trump endorsement. The president has endorsed in all House races, save for the open 6th District, which Rep. John W. Rose is vacating to run for governor. 

#FL07: Florida Reps. Anna Paulina Luna and Mike Haridopolos endorsed former news anchor Ryan Elijah’s primary challenge to fellow GOP Rep. Cory Mills, who is the subject of an Ethics Committee investigation. 

Democratic endorsements: Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg is backing Democrat Katy Padilla Stout in Texas’ 23rd District. New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill's Mission to Deliver PAC is endorsing 13 congressional hopefuls with military or national security backgrounds. They include candidates facing upcoming primaries such as Massachusetts Rep. Seth Moulton, who is challenging Sen. Edward J. Markey; Marine Corps veteran Maura Sullivan, who’s running for New Hampshire’s open 1st District; and Navy veteran and former NASA Chief of Staff Bale Dalton, who's seeking Florida's 7th District held by Republican Cory Mills.

#MESEN: Senate Majority PAC, a super PAC with ties to Senate Democratic leaders, released a poll Thursday that found Democrat Troy Jackson leading Maine Sen. Susan Collins, 49 percent to 45 percent with 6 percent undecided. The polling memo said that this year, Collins faces “a much more hostile political environment than she did in 2020.”

Missouri redistricting: Opponents of Missouri’s new GOP-drawn congressional map are suing after the Republican secretary of state blocked an effort to let voters weigh in on the new lines this fall, saying the challenge was unconstitutional. 

What we're reading

#FLSEN: Sen. Ashley Moody’s campaign to complete the Senate term she was appointed to last year when Marco Rubio became secretary of state is more low key than the races being run by other top Florida Republicans, Politico reports, and that has sparked some concerns by GOP operatives. Democrats hope that Alex Vindman, who has proved to be a strong fundraiser, can force a competitive race this fall.

Who will win the "orphaned" vote? Due to California’s nonpartisan primary system, the general elections in several key House races are one-party affairs, including the contest for the redrawn 40th District between Republican Reps. Young Kim and Ken Calvert. The Los Angeles Times looks at the strategic decisions “orphaned” Democratic voters are making about who to support. 

“Survival mode”: The Associated Press takes stock of DNC Chair Ken Martin as he fights to hold on to his job amid mounting frustration over how he handled a 2024 election “autopsy” report and the party’s financial struggles.

Courting Black conservatives: Capital B News examines Georgia Republican Rep. Mike Collins’ effort to win over Black voters in his challenge to Sen. Jon Ossoff. Collins’ quest comes as “questions about a member of his family’s white nationalist views – and the candidate’s own social media history – continue to generate negative headlines," the outlet reports.

An aging donor: The New York Times reports that Ronald Lauder, the cosmetics heir who has been a major donor for New York Republicans, seems to have cut off his political spending, raising questions within the state GOP of who might match his giving.

The count: 35 percent

That’s the share of Americans who profess to have no opinion on their district’s current candidates for Congress, according to a new Economist/YouGov poll.

That perhaps shouldn’t be surprising, given that 72 House districts – home to a total of nearly 36 million registered voters – won’t have an incumbent on the November ballot. That’s largely due to the abnormally high number of members willingly leaving the chamber, either to retire or seek other office, as well as those who resigned or lost their primaries.

In addition, redistricting in multiple states this cycle has thrown millions more voters in newly redrawn districts with a different House incumbent atop their ballot.– By Roll Call’s Ryan Kelly

Key race: #WI03

Candidates: Wisconsin GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden’s 3rd District seat is a top Democratic target this fall. National Democrats have largely lined up behind Rebecca Cooke, who unsuccessfully challenged Van Orden in 2024 and lost a Democratic primary for the seat in 2022. Also seeking the Democratic nomination is former Eau Claire City Council President Emily Berge. 

Why it matters: The battleground 3rd District is likely to be among the most competitive races this November, but Cooke, Democrats’ preferred candidate, must first get through Tuesday’s primary.

Cash dash: Cooke has been the race’s top fundraiser so far, bringing in $8.6 million through July 22, when she reported having $1.8 million on hand. Berge raised $729,000 and had $106,000 banked for the campaigns’ final stretch. Van Orden, meanwhile, reported raising $7.5 million this cycle and had $4.7 million on hand when he filed his pre-primary report last month. Outside groups have been active in the race over the past year. Law Enforcement for a Safer America PAC has spent $47,000 to support Van Orden, while the Wisco Project PAC, which mobilizes college students in the state, has spent $58,000 opposing his campaign. Pro-Choice Majority Action has spent $249,000 on ads supporting Cooke. And the Indivisible Project dropped $2,290 on a pro-Berge billboard. Meanwhile, Cooke has requested an extension on her personal financial disclosure that OpenSecrets reports has drawn criticism from both Berge and Van Orden.

Backers: The DCCC is backing Cooke, adding her to its Red to Blue program for promising candidates earlier this year. She’s also won endorsements from across the ideological spectrum, from the moderate Blue Dog PAC to progressives such as Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders and home-state Sen. Tammy Baldwin. Berge touts endorsements from several local leaders and the local Indivisible Coalition. Van Orden, as the incumbent, is backed by the traditional Republican groups. 

What they’re saying: In the Democratic primary, Berge has advocated more progressive policies such as “Medicare for All,” while Cooke said at a June forum that while she supports a public option, steps like restoring expired health insurance subsidies were a more likely approach for Democrats in Congress. Cooke has run ads highlighting her endorsement from Sanders, while another recent spot claims Van Orden “sold us out” on data centers. While Berge is the underdog in the primary, her campaign argues it’s gained momentum ahead of Tuesday’s primary and sees a path to victory. Van Orden, who hasn’t had to contend with a primary, has trained his attacks on Cooke, saying that she’s Democrats' "anointed" candidate and that he’s brought back important resources for the state as a member of Congress.

Terrain: The 3rd District is largely rural, covering parts of southwestern and western Wisconsin, including the cities Eau Claire and La Crosse. Trump carried the seat by 7 points in 2024, while Van Orden defeated Cooke by 3 points to win a second term. Inside Elections rates the race a Toss-up.

Wild cards: The 3rd District has become a popular destination for members of Trump’s Cabinet, many of whom have made appearances in the district this year, Politico reported. And a win for Francesca Hong in next week’s gubernatorial primary could complicate things for down-ballot Democrats trying to maintain some distance from the self-described democratic socialist, Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales wrote last week.

Tennessee is a rare state that holds its primaries on Thursdays for largely unknown reasons, and all eyes will be on Republican Rep. Andy Ogles as he faces off against his better-funded challenger. Meanwhile, Sen. Marsha Blackburn confronts Rep. John W. Rose and state Rep. Monty Fritts in her pursuit of the GOP seal of approval for her gubernatorial bid. And the Republican primaries for two open House seats – the GOP-held 6th District and newly deep-red 9th – will likely determine their next members of Congress. 

Photo finish

Former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford, with pigs in tow, returned to the State House in Columbia on Thursday to protest wasteful spending in the US government. The former congressman is running in next week’s special primary to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham on the GOP ticket. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

news.title: Is 'Communist' No Longer a Slur?
news.text:
It is not difficult, these days, to see the neo-communist flipside of "Democratic Socialists" — once they find power.

Indeed, the more the ossified Democratic Party claims that its growing cadre of socialist renegades are not really socialists, the more they act like — and even appear comfortable being called — communists.

With every new policy they propose, the socialists have been dropping the pretense that they are not Marxists.

How about declaring capitalism a failure?

All the socialists now do that — and even Democratic California Governor Gavin Newsom has also started agreeing that "capitalism as we know it doesn't work either." Oddly, Newsom himself, a multimillionaire and a beneficiary of arch-capitalist Gordon Getty's largesse, seems to have done quite well under capitalism.

Confiscating private property?

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani claims he will do just that if New York's landlords, in his opinion, are poor custodians of their own property.

Dismantling the U.S. Constitution?

Almost all Democrats have long called for destroying the 238-year-old Electoral College. And now the socialists openly brag that, when they take over the Democratic Party and then the nation, they will, as good Bolsheviks, go much further: destroying the Senate, destroying the Pentagon, destroying prisons, destroying the police, and destroying our borders.

And they want to take over utilities, break up or absorb corporate agriculture, and own major industries. Apparently, socialists believe that with a snap of their fingers they can destroy key elements of the U.S. constitutional order. Would these "socialists" even resent their agenda being called "communist"?

They also seem to have taken their cue for such radical change from "mainstream" Democrats — for example, Kamala Harris. Now in her third vain bid for the presidency, she has adopted the doctrine of "if you can't beat them, join them." So Harris now promises that if she is elected, she will pack the court, admit two new blue states (to snag four liberal senators), end the filibuster, and junk the Electoral College. How she plans to amend the Constitution to that effect she never tells us.

Like all good Marxists, these "ends-justify-the-means" leftists show an utter lack of principle: If two new red states wished to join the U.S., they would lecture us on the sanctity of a 50-state union. If they were a permanent Senate minority, they would, as in the past, honor the filibuster. If they had lost the popular vote in two recent elections but won the Electoral College, they would praise the wisdom of the Founders. If they had their Earl Warren-era majority again, they would laud the continuity of the 157-year-old nine-justice Supreme Court.

How about making "enemies of the people" lists and forcing sales of private property?

Mamdani just sent out a public list of nearly one million New York homeowners. He sent official warnings to 17,000 of these property owners that, if within four weeks they cannot prove that they have lived full-time in their own properties, the city will levy a huge surtax on them to drive home the point that no one should own an additional high-value home. Are show trials next for those who decline to reply?

In other words, Mamdani has flipped the American tradition of "innocent until proven guilty." Instead, almost 20,000 New Yorkers are now automatically presumed guilty of being house-hoarding, capitalist leeches who owe the exploited classes tens of thousands of dollars a year in reparations, unless they — the newly presumed guilty — can prove themselves innocent.

Welcome to Mamdani's revolutionary court.

Mamdani's new surtax could add from $40,000 to $350,000 a year to tens of thousands of homeowners' taxes — in addition to already-existing steep property taxes that often range from $5,000 to $150,000.

Most owners will do the math and see that the new aggregate tax payouts in just a few years could be more than the value of the home itself.

Why is Mamdani doing this?

The socialist mayor's aim here seems twofold:

First, he wants to flush out and dox anyone owning two homes as a purported enemy of the people.

And so, Mamdani created a list of his targets, including their addresses, and published it. To the extent that many properties really were second homes, Mamdani has now made sure that all New Yorkers, including envious rubberneckers, would-be squatters, and hardened criminals, know exactly where they might target a sometimes-vacant home.

Second, he wants to force a massive fire sale of second homes that would crash home values in general and so redistribute now "affordable" houses to those whom Mamdani considers, as victims of capitalism, to be more deserving of these properties.

Recently, on cable news, the national co-chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, Megan Romer, was asked a series of questions about her group's published agenda. Far from denying its communist radicalism, she gleefully confirmed it all — from destroying the border to ending prisons, the military, and the police.

But it is in Spain, and Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's corrupt and unpopular regime, where we see what one-eyed-jack socialists can do when they are finally in power, especially when they are hated and on their way out.

Sanchez has given amnesty to 600,000 illegal aliens. One result was that 60,000 Muslim men from North Africa in a single day recently swarmed Spain's colonial outpost on the Moroccan coast at Ceuta, demanding amnesties and free subsidized passes into European Spain — while looting and vandalizing businesses and attacking Spaniards.

So why do European socialists and American leftists, once elected, destroy borders, create conditions of mass chaos, and welcome in millions of illegal aliens — poor, often angry, and unassimilated — from the Third World?

Aside from their belief that the capitalists and their bourgeois hirelings deserve chaos, violence, and upheaval, they hate the fact that capitalism is too class-fluid to furnish a permanent exploited proletarian underclass.

And so they import a huge victim class, and virtue signal their purported moral superiority. Then they spend lavish social largesse upon the influx, and, in quid pro quo fashion, thus bind their imported underclass with their welfare-state assurances.

Mail-in and early ballots, no-ID voting, same-day registration, ballot harvesting and curing, and no final verdicts on Election Day were all leftist projects, all designed to enroll as many illegal voters as possible.

The Left has also learned from experience that the time between immigrant parents fleeing third-world hellholes to find safety, freedom, and prosperity in the U.S. and their children hating the very generous host that welcomed them — and demanding that America be radically transformed to resemble the catastrophe from which they or their parents fled — is often only about 20 years.

So if one enjoys watching the careers of Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib, AOC, or Mamdani, then one should certainly vote socialist to ensure that they are the new model for American elected officials.

It is the paradox of our age that anyone can flee Somalia, the West Bank, Puerto Rico, or Uganda and then win the global lottery by being accepted into America's constitutional society and free-market economy — only to do their best to repay the generosity of their host by turning their new country into something unrecognizable to the prior 10 generations of Americans.

But then again, America might become quite similar to the mess they abandoned.

So far, the model holds true: Socialist candidates (as opposed to registered socialist activists) hide their communist-adjacent agendas during elections. But once in office and drunk with power, they find socialism too wishy-washy and go full communist. So they destroy borders, institutions, names, dates, statues, norms, customs, and traditions to replicate the illiberalism and concomitant failures of a new Haiti, a West Bank, or a Morocco in the West.

In sum, to make a new socialist America, you must first destroy everything that made Americans and all that they hold dear.

news.title: Now We Have Proof the Democrats' Anti-Trump Lawfare Was Never About the Law
news.text:
Long before Donald Trump took the oath of office for his second term — heck, before he was even reelected — Democrat state attorneys general were already building the machine designed to stop him.

Records show that at least 22 Democrat attorneys general joined a coalition called the Project for Federal Accountability starting in April 2024, roughly seven months before Trump defeated Kamala Harris. Seven attorneys general signed the agreement on April 28, 2024. Thirteen more joined in May and June.

The pact was called "Privileged & Confidential Common Interest Agreement." It was built to do exactly what it sounds like: Keep the states' coordination hidden from the public and from anyone who might dare oppose them in court. The signers said they wanted to pursue their shared legal interests "while avoiding any waiver of the confidentiality of those privileged materials." Translation: Total secrecy while colluding against a sitting president who hadn't even taken office yet.

To me, the most significant part of this pact is that Biden was still in the race when the first signatures went on that agreement in April 2024. He wouldn't drop out for nearly three months. The sitting Democrat president was telling the country he intended to serve another term, the party was acting like he was going to win, all while Democrat attorneys general were already plotting to stop Trump upon his inevitable return to office.

ICYMI: Did a Democrat Senator Accidentally Admit He Knows That Fauci Broke the Law?

The coalition had already divided up legal research by topic, built a shared "brief bank" of pre-drafted briefs, and pored over the Project 2025 policy blueprint hunting for lawsuit targets. Trump hadn't signed a bill. He hadn't issued an executive order. He hadn't taken any official action as president, because he wasn't president yet. None of that mattered. The lawsuits were already being written.

Since Trump's second term began, Democrat attorneys general have sued his administration close to 100 times. California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D-Calif.) has taken part in 82 of those lawsuits. Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser (D-Colo.) has joined at least 75. Washington Attorney General Nick Brown (D-Wash.) has joined 70.

Bonta insists the coalition's work is "apolitical." Seriously? He also said, "If (Trump) doesn't want to get sued, all he has to do is follow the law," adding, "I don't think our cases are likely to be dismissed... Trump shows no sign of slowing down, so we will continue to sue him."

Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown (D-Md.) claims the early coordination was reasonable preparation once Trump's nomination looked inevitable, but this confirms that the strategy was always about resistance, not the rule of law.

Even people outside the conservative media world find this strange. Retired Connecticut judge Thomas Moukawsher mocked the coalition's chosen name: "'Federal Accountability?' That's just a little strange." 

Former Utah Attorney General Mark Shurtleff, a Republican who now often votes for Democrats, called the secrecy “not normal at all."

California alone has burned through $19 million in taxpayer money on this litigation crusade, with another $25 million already authorized. New Jersey tucked $1 million into its fiscal year 2026 budget just to fund two new staff positions dedicated to the coalition's work. That’s right, taxpayers are literally footing the bill for a legal ambush that was planned before Trump even won the election. Imagine all the other things California could have wasted more money on. Democrats can claim all they want that this is about accountability and the rule of law, but it’s just blanket resistance.

And if you live in a blue state, you’re paying for it.
