news.title: What Gen Z’s dark humor really says about their values
news.text:
After Luigi Mangione was arrested in December 2024 in connection with the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, the internet did what it often does: It turned something serious into a joke.

Although Mangione has pleaded not guilty to second-degree murder in New York and to federal stalking charges, viral memes at the time romanticized him as a popular – and incredibly attractive – man of the people who made corporate elites within the American health insurance industry afraid.

Some of these memes adhered to conventional forms of political satire. One, for example, quoted a speech from the movie “A Bug’s Life,” in which a villainous grasshopper argues for the need to punish the movie’s ant protagonist to keep the other ants in line. In this meme, the political point was clear: Elites preserve power by making examples of insignificant ants who dare to challenge them.

The point was less clear with other memes, including celebrations of Mangione’s fashion-forward shackled ankles in court and mock Burger King advertisements referencing the fact that a McDonald’s employee had been the one to call law enforcement on him: “Burger King: We won’t turn you in to the Feds.” Rather than being ironic, they are unserious.

Nonetheless, memes like those received serious reactions from social commentators and political pundits who interpreted them as evidence that America’s young adults are nihilistic and morally indifferent.

As an experimental psychologist who studies moral judgments about real-world controversies, I have examined these attitudes toward Mangione and the humor surrounding him online.

I believe these reactions are better understood not as a rejection of value but as a refusal to participate in conversations that feel selective and disconnected from young people’s broader economic and political frustrations. In my assessment, Gen Z’s dark and nonsensical humor does not show a lack of moral values, but it’s instead the product of its desire to engage in more authentic conversations about what they believe.

Research shows deep levels of alienation among Gen Z, or young adults born between 1997 and 2012. Having grown up with smartphones and social media, this generation has come of age in an increasingly online world. Despite the internet’s capacity for instantaneous interaction, followers have proved a poor replacement for friends.

Gen Z is among the most socially isolated and psychologically distressed generations on record. Compared with prior generations, fewer friendships and romantic relationships have left many young adults craving connection and solidarity. This alienation is also evident in their skepticism toward institutions and traditional narratives about values.

Many are pessimistic about achieving the American Dream and question the value of higher education. What was once considered the optimal vehicle for living a better life is instead viewed as a barrier.

If the American Dream feels out of reach, and college seems like an expensive obstacle, calls to take them seriously may feel inauthentic, alienating and absurd.

Discussions about values require some seriousness if they are to resonate with their audience.

If, for example, a commencement speaker praising the value of artificial intelligence is met with jeers from graduates – as former Google CEO Eric Schmidt was in May 2026 – the speaker’s message is immediately rendered inert.

These students’ jeers fell short of offering an argument against the speaker’s claims; instead, they created an atmosphere that prevented those claims from receiving consideration. For graduates pessimistic about AI’s implications for the labor market, claims professing its value feel inauthentic.

Together, their jeers not only provided an escape from what felt like an alienating and inauthentic message about the value of AI, but they also created a sense of solidarity through a shared suspension of seriousness.

Far from being unique to Mangione, this suspension of seriousness recurs throughout online meme culture.

The OceanGate implosion prompted similar memes, including one depicting a pod of orcas with the caption “The water is safe, send more billionaires.”

Even Charlie Kirk’s assassination became material. In a trend known as “Kirkification,” users superimposed his face onto images ranging from the Mona Lisa to women in bikinis, transforming a grim event into a shared absurdity.

In my assessment, Gen Z’s creation and circulation of memes offers an escape from otherwise serious conversations – for example, conversations about the value of the UnitedHealthcare CEO’s life. This may be especially true when demands to condemn Mangione appear to ignore inequities within an American health insurance system perceived as corrupt and unjust.

Although commentators often dismiss Gen Z’s humor as nonsensical or nihilistic meme slop, scholarship suggests that it acts as a collaborative coping mechanism, driven by a desire for authenticity.

Memes about Mangione, or even campus lookalike contests centered on him, fall short of offering a precise moral argument in favor of largely suspending seriousness.

This style of humor can be seen in Mangione’s alleged decision to leave a backpack containing Monopoly money in Central Park. It was seen, too, on shell casings recovered after Kirk’s killing, which included video game commands, a sexually suggestive internet saying and “if you read this you are gay lmao.”

With the help of approximately a dozen undergraduate students, I examined the psychological and situational factors associated with Gen Z’s reactions to Mangione and other events – like Kirk’s assassination and the Kamala Harris is “Brat” phenomenon during the 2024 presidential election – in two studies currently under review.

Our findings indicate that favorable attitudes toward Mangione were associated not only with superficial factors, such as his perceived attractiveness, but also with higher levels of political cynicism.

Perceived systemic bias in the American justice system, for example, was addressed in a meme depicting Mangione walking into court with the text “You can kill dozens of kids and get a lesser sentence because their lives don’t matter as much as a CEO’s.” Federal prosecutors were seeking the death penalty against Mangione for a charge a judge dismissed in January 2026.

Casting Gen Z’s reactions as nihilistic obscures the values and institutional distrust connected to them and fails to appreciate their egalitarian and pragmatic ideals. Dismissing them may deepen the alienation that allowed the death of a father of two to become a joke.

Although political commentators disagree about how to interpret the response to Mangione, many accept a seemingly basic principle: Killing should never be justified.

Yet decades of research on moral judgment shows that people do not apply that principle consistently. Instead, in certain situations, like in the famous “trolley problem,” people frequently judge killing to be morally permissible – especially when that killing is expected to promote the well-being of others.

Simplistic and sweeping moral injunctions not only fail to appreciate people’s actual moral attitudes, but they also eliminate the possibility of having authentic and nuanced conversations.

Those conversations need not end by endorsing Mangione as a sympathetic figure. However, an open and authentic conversation about Mangione cannot be realized in spaces that require all discussion of the event to be reduced to affirmations that, as has been advocated by some, “Murder is bad. Period.”

Such requirements can make conversations about significant moral issues – even controversial ones, like the morality of Mangione’s alleged actions – little more than demands for conformity. In this case, those boundaries risk ignoring and, thus, further alienating, Gen Z.

Gen Z’s humor shows that almost anything can become a joke. I believe the danger of that is not that young people reject values, but that continued alienation may leave them laughing when seriousness is most required.
news.summary: Having grown up with smartphones and social media, this generation has come of age in an increasingly online world

news.title: Socialists are doing a Trump to the Democrats. US politics is unlikely to return to normal
news.text:
To give you a sense of it, consider Darializa Avila Chevalier, one of the DSA members to win a Democrat primary. “F!@# Kamala Harris” she tweeted when Harris was vice president. A year prior she’d called Joe Biden a “rapist”. When Chevalier won her New York primary, a former Bill Clinton aide said the party “should not seat her in the caucus” because she is “not a democrat”. Another establishment Democrat was moved to post: “if you hate the Democratic Party, then please don’t run for our nomination. Don’t use our resources. Don’t rely on our volunteers. Don’t use our infrastructure. Focus on building the party you actually support.” The establishment senses this is not an evolution, it’s a takeover bid.

That’s because Donald Trump has thoroughly changed the political game. Most obviously, he’s shown it’s possible to seize control of a major party, and remake it in a once unthinkable image. But he also lit a fire under progressives who sought a takeover of their own, and took inspiration from Bernie Sanders. When Trump first entered office, the DSA had an influx of tens of thousands of new, young members. That plateaued when Biden became president, but Trump’s second victory has brought the energy back. And this energy isn’t just threatening to transform the Democrats. It’s transforming the very DSA that is currently besieging it.

The DSA was established in the ’80s with the aim of pulling the Democratic Party in a more progressive direction. It was socialist – committed to bringing about the end of capitalism – but also anti-communist. It upheld liberty, free speech, and free elections. It specifically banned communists from becoming members. But the post-Trump influx contained a new hardcore of genuine communists and Marxist-Leninists. The past decade has been one of internal DSA ructions, with some of its founding members leaving in protest. One Marxist-Leninist faction, called the Red Star caucus, now boasts that “nearly half” of the members of the DSA’s highest leadership body “openly identify as communists”. Meanwhile, the DSA officially removed its ban on communist members.

As a result, the DSA is now divided in its aims. One group retains the old vision of influencing the Democrats. Another wants to establish a separate party and fight them. A third group wants to run candidates in Democrat primaries, win new members to the DSA and then break away and form a new party, leaving a shell of a Democratic Party in its wake.
news.summary: Donald Trump has changed the political game. He’s shown it’s possible to seize control of a major party and remake it.

news.title: Impeachment articles filed against 'unelected shadow president'
news.text:
A House Democrat on Thursday introduced articles of impeachment against White House budget chief Russell Vought, accusing the Project 2025 architect and far-right ideologue of unlawfully terminating federal funds appropriated by Congress and putting the Trump administration’s political priorities over the law.

Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif.), who is leading the push to remove Vought, pointed to his partisan cancellation of federal funding for Democratic-led states as “just the latest example” of illegal and impeachable conduct.

“Vought has repeatedly and openly broken the law to stroke Trump’s fragile ego,” Kamlager-Dove said in a statement. “These nakedly partisan schemes to punish Democratic voters ultimately hurt families and workers of all political stripes. We cannot sit idly by while an unelected shadow president continues to weaponize the federal government and steal taxpayers’ hard-earned money. Russell Vought’s blatant abuse of power and complete disregard for the Constitution warrants immediate removal by Congress.”

Kamlager-Dove filed two articles of impeachment against Vought, who has quietly become one of the most powerful and influential figures in the second Trump administration. One of the new articles accuses the White House budget director of “abuse of power through improper impoundment of congressionally appropriated funds,” and the other alleges “failure to faithfully execute the laws of the United States.”

Last month, Trump administration officials admitted in court filings that they terminated billions of dollars worth of Biden-era federal grants for clean energy projects in some states “based solely” on political considerations, including whether former Vice President Kamala Harris won the state in the 2024 election.

“Such conduct represents an unconstitutional interference with Congress’ exclusive authority over appropriations and an abuse of executive power,” states Kamlager-Dove’s first impeachment article against Vought.

The California Democrat launched her impeachment push as Vought worked to place billions of dollars in federal grant money under the control of political appointees, a change that scientists, environmental groups, and other critics say would leave funding for key research at the mercy of the Trump administration’s political whims.

“The proposed rule would systematically politicize federal funding and allow Trump officials to cancel grants at any time for any reason,” Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) said this past weekend. “Enabling this rule would only give [President Donald] Trump the green light to take even more federal funding hostage.”

“While Republicans rejected killing the proposed rule outright, I’m going to keep fighting to put a stop to it once and for all, and I will keep pressing my Republican colleagues to do exactly that,” said Murray.

news.title: Jill Biden Says She Doesn't Think She'll See a Female President in Her Lifetime — and Admits Being 'Shocked' Kamala Harris Lost to Trump
news.text:
Jill Biden doesn't think she will see a female president in her lifetime, RadarOnline.com can reveal, less than two years after she watched Donald Trump defeat Kamala Harris in the presidential election.

The former First Lady appeared on SiriusXM’s Let's Talk Off Camera with Kelly Ripa and discussed whether a woman will ever be Commander-in-Chief.'I Feel Like Probably Not in My Lifetime'"Do you think we'll ever see a woman president in our lifetimes?" the talk show host asked Jill, as she responded, "In my lifetime? I'm 75. I feel like probably not in my lifetime, Kelly, but maybe in yours."

Jill then recalled Harris' unexpected loss to Trump, and noted, "I really did think last time that Kamala was gonna win. I was out on the campaign trail for her. I saw the excitement, I saw the crowds, I saw it at the convention. 

"I saw all the energy, and I thought, 'Finally, we're going to have a woman president.'"

The 75-year-old added, "And I must tell you, I was shocked the morning after when I got up at 5:00 in the morning to feed Willow and get ready for the day, and I found out that she had lost. Shocked."Jill Biden V. Kamala HarrisJill, who previously suggested Harris "would be a good president," is rumored to have had a feud with the ex-veep behind the scenes.

In her memoir, View From the East Wing, Jill touches on the moment her husband, Joe Biden, decided to step down from the presidency. During an interview, journalist Paola Ramos shared, "There's this one moment in the book that I think a lot of people are talking about, when you describe that when President Biden was talking about stepping down and endorsing her, you walk out. You walk out of the room because she wanted an immediate endorsement, and you storm out."

However, Jill pushed back on Ramos' choice of words, responding, "I didn't say storm... Joe had made the decision to drop out. It was very emotional, you might well imagine." Harris would end up taking over for Joe and battling it out against Trump.

In Harris' memoir, 107 Days, she noted the lack of support she felt she received from Jill and Joe and their inner circle while running in 2024.'I Want It Sooner'"And when the stories were unfair or inaccurate, the president's inner circle seemed fine with it... It seemed as if they decided I should be knocked down a little bit more," she claimed in her book. According to Harris, it was Jill who pushed her husband to stay in the race following his disastrous debate performance against Trump.

She noted, "It's Joe and Jill's decision. We all said that, like a mantra, as if we'd all been hypnotized. Was it grace, or was it recklessness? In retrospect, I think it was recklessness."

Joe dropped out on July 21, 2024, and in her memoir, Jill claimed Harris was eager for an endorsement, as she allegedly said, "Oh my God, Joe. Are you sure?"

After Joe made it clear he wanted to wait until morning to endorse her, Jill claimed Harris demanded, "I want it sooner."According to Jill, after her husband said he'd give Harris a call "when I figure this out," she allegedly pressed him, "Could you do it soon? Say, in 20 minutes?" 

Harris' behavior led Jill to leave the room. The 61-year-old has not confirmed whether she will be running for president, as according to sources, "She hasn’t ruled it out. No credible strategist would recommend ruling it out this early.

"But she also understands that the window to make the case that her vision and leadership in elected office is what this moment requires isn't open indefinitely."
news.summary: Jill Biden has admitted she doesn't think America will elect a female president in her lifetime.
news.author: Bryan Brunati

news.title: Mark Ruffalo says his Kia is 'hands down a better car' than a Tesla: 'Feels luxury'
news.text: Mark Ruffalo took a shot at Tesla. "I mean… they are not well made cars," he wrote on X on Wednesday while sharing an Autoblog article about a preliminary NHTSA investigation into Tesla. Instead, the actor, best-known for playing Bruce Banner in "The Avengers," said he prefers an EV from a Korean automaker that built its name on budget-friendly vehicles. "Having tucked into a KIA EV now and having driven a Tesla," Ruffalo said. "I have to say the Kia is hands down a better car and feels luxury compared to a Tesla." I mean… they are not well made cars. Having tucked into a KIA EV now and having driven a Tesla. I have to say the Kia is hands down a better car and feels luxury compared to a Tesla. https://t.co/v10NorXy1Q Ruffalo has a long history with electric vehicles and Tesla. In 2012, he said he had placed a deposit on a Model S and described himself as number 6,345 on the car's waiting list. He also tweeted in support of the automaker in 2014 when New York State considered banning Tesla because it sold directly to consumers. The actor's views of Tesla CEO Elon Musk have since soured. Tensions between Musk and Ruffalo surfaced in 2022, when the actor said Musk was destroying his credibility after taking over Twitter. Ruffalo also campaigned for Kamala Harris in 2024, while Musk spent at least $270 million supporting Donald Trump and other Republicans during that election cycle. NHTSA's preliminary investigation covers nearly 1.2 million Model 3 and Model Y vehicles. The agency said it received 156 complaints alleging that a front suspension component detached, and said the alleged failures could cause a "loss of vehicle directional control." No related crashes, injuries, or deaths were known when the investigation was opened, and the probe has not resulted in a recall. Representatives for Ruffalo, Kia, and Tesla didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.
news.summary: The actor and longtime environmental activist criticized Tesla's build quality while praising Kia's EV.

news.title: Democrats targeting 12 additional red districts in midterms push to retake House

news.title: Trump-supporting Miss North Carolina USA STRIPPED of title over problematic posts
news.text:
The group behind the Miss North Carolina USA contest says the decision to strip the title from 27-year-old Brittany Boltinhouse was a "difficult" one.

The Mexican-Honduran model from Beulaville posted messages years ago that the organization said went against its values. 

She had warned that voting for Kamala Harris would risk turning America into a 'third world country.'

Boltinhouse is also a supporter of President Donald Trump, though that wasn't included in the organization's statement.

"This decision was not made lightly," the organizers said on Instagram. "It followed a thorough review of recently surfaced information and was based on the totality of the circumstances and our responsibility to preserve the integrity of the Miss North Carolina USA title and the values of our organization."

The posts were not included, but the NC Beat documented that Boltinhouse used the N-word numerous times between 2017 and 2018, and referred to herself as "toxic."

She had warned that voting for Kamala Harris would risk turning America into a "third world country" in another post and also shared a photograph of herself at a Trump rally, according to the Beat.

The discovery led to backlash from some who objected to her posts and called her a "self-hating, Trump-supporting, racist, ignorant women [sic] who does not speak for me or for any of the other ACTUAL PROUD HISPANAS." 

Miss USA Chairman and CEO Thom Brodeur said that "racism, homophobia, transphobia, [and] language that strips any person of their dignity" are against the organization's values, but it's unclear if he was referring to her posts or her support of the president. 

"As an organization entrusted with selecting and preparing women to represent our states on the national stage," the organization continued, "we must uphold the standards and values that our titleholders agree to embrace when accepting the honor of wearing the crown."

The incident is even more bizarre considering that Trump once owned the Miss USA pageant before he became president.

Myla Hadley, the runner-up in the pageant contest, will take up the mantle of Miss North Carolina USA 2026.

Boltinhouse was the first Honduran model to win the Miss North Carolina USA title.

news.title: EXCLUSIVE: Inside Trump's Feuds With Pop Stars After Katy Perry Joined Hit List
news.text:
Donald Trump is still locked in a new front in his long campaign of cultural combat – a rolling war against some of the world's biggest pop stars, whose music he borrows for his own political ends while publicly deriding them when they push back.

As RadarOnline.com readers know, the US president, 80, is now waging war in Iran and threatening invasions of Canada, Greenland, Cuba, Colombia and Panama, and has also ordered strikes in Syria, Somalia, Iraq, Yemen and Nigeria. 

But some of his most personal battles have played out not on foreign soil but in the glare of the entertainment world, as he clashes with Katy Perry, Taylor Swift, Bruce Springsteen, Madonna, Beyoncé – and a long list of other musicians who have denounced his policies or blocked him from using their songs.Katy Perry Clashes With TrumpPerry was thrust into Trump's crosshairs last week after the White House used her 2010 hit Firework as the soundtrack to a video montage of military strikes titled "Iran has been warned."

As Perry sang "Boom! Boom! Boom!," the video showed bombs exploding. 

She said: "To see a message of self-worth and upliftment weaponised to soundtrack destruction and violence is a complete violation of everything my song stands for."

Perry added her music was supposed to be "for bringing people together, not celebrating warfare."

The 41-year-old singer's comments have sparked a fresh round of presidential recriminations.

Trump removed Firework from his video – only to retaliate by posting footage of Perry in military fatigues holding a weapon, spliced between images of Trump and fighter jets. 

The rage came as the clip, taken from one of Perry's old music videos, was repurposed to suggest she was aligned with his hardline stance. 

A senior political source exclusively told Radar: "If Katy Perry wants to lecture us about peace, she shouldn't be surprised when we remind people she once played a soldier on screen."Taylor Swift Draws Trump's FurySwift's decision to endorse Democratic candidate Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential race marked another turning point in Trump's war on music's biggest names. 

After months of publicly courting the singer's vote, Trump erupted online: "I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!" 

He posted the outburst on social media, and has also raged online: "Has anyone noticed that, since I said 'I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT,' she's no longer 'HOT?'" This came despite Swift headlining a record-breaking world tour and releasing blockbuster albums. 

One Harris campaign aide said: "Trump went from begging for her approval to belittling her success the moment she chose democracy over him."

Beyoncé has also become a target. 

Trump falsely claimed she had been paid $10million to endorse Harris and appear at a 2024 rally in Houston, Texas, alleging the performer "left the stage to a booing and angry audience" – even though her event company received only $165,000 to cover costs and video evidence showed no jeering. 

Trump escalated the feud last year, saying Beyoncé and every celebrity who backed Harris "should all be prosecuted." 

A source close to Beyoncé said: "Trump tries to criminalise dissent – if you're not singing for him, he wants you silenced."More Stars Hit BackThe pattern extends beyond those who criticise him outright.

The White House used Puerto Rican rapper Bad Bunny's song La Mudanza in a video showing federal agents handcuffing immigrants, in a move insiders acknowledge was designed to antagonise the Super Bowl headliner.

Trump called the artist "absolutely terrible, one of the worst, EVER," and "an affront to the Greatness of America," complaining by singing in Spanish, "nobody understands a word this guy is saying," despite tens of millions of Spanish speakers in the US alone.

Other stars have reacted angrily when their songs surfaced in Trump's output.

Ariana Grande was outraged when her track Bye backed a White House video of immigration arrests.

She wrote on social media: "Please do not ever use my music in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense."

Sabrina Carpenter saw her song Juno turned into a soundtrack to another immigration clip, branding it "evil and disgusting." She added: "Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda."

Kesha called the White House administration "perverts" in February after her 2011 song Blow appeared on a Trump TikTok video of missile strikes titled Lethality.White House Defends StrategyOne Washington insider told us: "By provoking stars and leaning on their work without permission, Trump and his team court outrage and viral attention – it's a classic bid to try and stay relevant across all age groups online."

White House communications director Steven Cheung said: "All these 'singers' keep falling for this. This just gives us more attention and more view counts to our videos because people want to see what they're bitching about." 

Our Washington insider added: "For Trump, the backlash from pop royalty is just another battlefront – and the noise is part of the strategy."
news.summary: The list of Donald Trump's feuds with pop stars has been growing after Katy Perry joined the list.

news.title: Trump team to hand out $3B in ‘BIDEN’ grants – for communities that help deport more migrants
news.text:
The Department of Justice is making $3 billion available in grants to communities that agree to cooperate with federal immigration forces carrying out President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.

The Bridging Immigration-related Deficits Experienced Nationwide (or, BIDEN) Program was established – and spitefully named after former president Joe Biden – in last year's One Big Beautiful Bill, making the money available for distribution through September 2028.

One of the biggest offerings ever made by the DOJ, according to The Washington Post, the program is intended to bolster immigration enforcement by encouraging greater cooperation between state and federal authorities.

A 21-page introductory document explains that the funding is intended for "locating and apprehending aliens who have committed a crime under federal, state, or local law, in addition to being unlawfully present in the United States."

Jurisdictions that apply for the money have to agree to "fully participate" in the ICE 287(g) partnership, which brings together local police forces with immigration agents, and with the Homeland Security Task Force.

However, should their applications prove successful, they may spend their grant at their own discretion, so long as it goes towards hiring and training law enforcement personnel, investing in new crimefighting technology such as drones, body cameras and surveillance systems and building new temporary detention centers.

Jurisdictions do not need to prove that they were harmed directly by Biden administration immigration policies in order to qualify, only demonstrate a willingness to support Trump-backed enforcement efforts.

They will, however, be expected to commit to reimbursing "the costs associated with federal law enforcement intervention" should that later become necessary "to reduce crime or public disorder" related to the crackdown.

"This Department of Justice is committed to ensuring Biden-era border disasters never happen again," Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in a statement introducing the program, underlining the highly partisan nature of the offering.

"We are proud to once again champion law and order."

Former New Jersey attorney general Matthew Platkin, a Democrat, scorned the strategy, telling the Post: "Even the name of the grant itself is a political statement that is holding critical funds hostage to achieve goals they haven't been able to through legal means.

"It's a slap in the face to law enforcement."

The DOJ issued its first call for applications last month and has further funding rounds planned for August and September.

The department says it has already received 181 applications in the first 30 days, according to the Post, which considers that a slow start given the generosity of the offering but says that demand is likely to pick up over the coming months.

Trump was returned to power in November 2024 promising mass deportations, scaremongering during the campaign about "migrant crime" and pet-eating Haitians in Ohio and blaming Biden and Kamala Harris for allowing in "stone-cold killers."

Immigration and Customs Enforcement was subsequently greatly expanded under the leadership of former Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem and sent into Democrat-run cities such as Los Angeles and Chicago to round-up people suspected of being in the country illegally, inspiring widespread protests and a slew of negative stories about its activities.

However, the deaths of two protesters during Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis in January forced a rethink, with Noem and Border Patrol chief Greg Bovino removed and border czar Tom Homan placed in overall charge.

Noem was replaced by Oklahoma Republican senator Markwayne Mullin, who has already reportedly been the subject of "growing tensions" with the White House after ordering ICE to pause traffic stops following the deaths of two more people in Maine and Texas.
news.author: Joe Sommerlad

news.title: The Left’s Fake Conversion To Religious Liberty
news.text:
The progressive legal establishment for years treated religious freedom exemptions as obstacles to be dismantled, threatening the livelihoods, consciences, and institutions of Christian business owners, healthcare workers, and even nuns.

Now, the left is embracing the very religious-liberty arguments it spent years working to defeat.

Religious exemptions have typically rested on one of two legal foundations: the First Amendment’s protection of religious exercise or the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, which requires the government to justify substantial burdens on religious practice under the strictest level of judicial scrutiny.

This shift on the left is not merely rhetorical. Hoosier Jews for Choice has sued for religious exemptions from Indiana’s abortion ban, arguing that the law conflicts with Jewish teachings about when life begins. The Latino Christian National Network and other Christian and Jewish organizations have invoked religious freedom in challenges to ICE enforcement near houses of worship and in efforts to protect faith groups that shelter illegal immigrants.

Safehouse, a Philadelphia nonprofit, is likewise pressing a religious-liberty claim for permission to operate a supervised drug-consumption site. The organization argues that its Judeo-Christian obligation to preserve life and care for the sick entitles it to an exemption from federal drug laws. Together, the cases show progressive organizations adopting the same legal protections their political allies have long sought to narrow when invoked by conservative Christians, according to The Guardian. 

Constitutional and policy scholars, however, told the Caller the sudden pivot isn’t a genuine defense of conscience — it’s a tactical workaround that falls apart under legal scrutiny. (RELATED: EXCLUSIVE: Trump’s DOJ Sues Blue County Over Gun Ban In Churches)

Josh Blackman, a constitutional law professor at South Texas College of Law Houston, told the Caller that many of the cases are “silly and cynical,” but legally shrewd.

He said the strategy emerged as it became clear the Supreme Court would overturn Roe v. Wade in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, returning abortion policy to the states.

“Abortion is so important to the left, they had to find some way of protecting it, and they’ll use whatever tools are available,” Blackman said. “They replaced due process with an appeal to religion.”

Blackman added that the claims also give progressives a way to accuse conservatives of hypocrisy for supporting religious-liberty protections in earlier cases while questioning their use now.

Many earlier religious-liberty cases involved objections to government compulsion: a Christian baker declining to create a cake for a same-sex wedding, for example, or nuns resisting a mandate to provide contraceptive coverage.

The newer cases, by contrast, use religious-liberty claims to advance policy outcomes their proponents already supported on secular grounds. That distinction has led legal scholars such as Blackman to question whether the newfound commitment to religious freedom is principled or merely strategic.

Blackman, who has followed the Jewish abortion litigation for four years, said the plaintiffs may struggle to establish both the sincerity of their asserted beliefs and standing to sue — particularly where some of the women bringing the cases are not pregnant.

But, Blackman noted, “the problem is courts are very, very hesitant to probe sincerity.”

“The left is throwing everything against the wall to see what sticks,” Ethics and Public Policy Center President Ryan T. Anderson told the Caller, adding that “they have unfortunately not developed any newfound respect for religious freedom.”

Anderson said the left’s religious liberty claims are hardly comparable to those of the baker or nun, and instead “make a mockery of religious liberty.”

He compared the effort to self-described Satanists who claim a religious liberty right to obtain abortions, adding that “the attempts to use religious liberty protections to attack basic human rights protections for the unborn should be as successful as religious liberty claims to kill any other class of human beings.”

Anderson said many of the progressive religious liberty claims are opportunistic, noting that “they will ultimately fail either because the purported religious belief is not sincere or because the government has a truly compelling interest being pursued in the least restrictive way.”

The left’s new strategy marks a sharp departure from its earlier efforts to force religious groups to yield to progressive policy priorities, including repeated attempts to pass the Do No Harm Act across six consecutive Congresses — an effort championed in part by Kamala Harris during her Senate tenure.

The bill would have barred individuals and organizations from invoking RFRA to seek exemptions from federal laws governing civil rights, employment, healthcare and other areas where advocates argued religious claims could enable discrimination. Harris said the First Amendment’s guarantee of religious freedom should “never be used to undermine other Americans’ civil rights or subject them to discrimination on the basis of race, gender, sexual orientation, or gender identity.”

The legislative push followed a major setback for progressives in Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, in which the Supreme Court ruled that certain corporations could not be compelled under the Affordable Care Act to provide contraceptive coverage if doing so would violate their religious beliefs.

After failing to substantially narrow those protections through Congress, progressive advocates are now turning to the courts to invoke the same religious-liberty doctrines on behalf of abortion access, immigration sanctuaries and supervised drug-consumption sites.

While the left’s legal strategy may have changed, Anderson said its underlying goals have not “evolved,” pointing to New York state’s recent effort to force Roman Catholic nuns to participate in assisted suicide.

Blackman said most of the cases appear to be political or philosophical disputes recast in religious terms. Still, some could succeed if courts are reluctant to apply religious-liberty protections less generously to progressive plaintiffs than they did to conservatives in earlier cases. (RELATED: FBI, DEA Withhold Court-Ordered Files On Nigerian President’s Alleged Drug Trafficking Ahead Of Trump Meeting)

Progressive plaintiffs now stand on the opposite side of a religious-liberty debate that has divided the left and right for more than a decade. Their lawsuits will test how broadly protections once associated with conservative causes apply when invoked in pursuit of progressive ones.
news.summary: ‘A mockery of religious liberty’

news.title: JD Vance trolls online critics with expletives, personal insults
news.text:
WASHINGTON >> It was hardly the first time that someone on social media called someone else fat. But it may have been the first time that a vice president of the United States did so.

Peeved at a conservative columnist who criticized his position on Iran, Vice President JD Vance jabbed on Wednesday at his physical appearance. “If you’ve ever met him in person,” he wrote on social media, “it’s quite obvious the man has never missed a burrito.”

In an era when playground insults pass for political dialogue, few have leaped into the online flame wars with more gusto than Vance. The first millennial vice president has long dispensed with the decorum and restraint of his older predecessors to go after the “idiots” and “scumbags” who anger him, from the “limousine socialists” on the left to the “disgraceful” conservatives on the right.

He works, of course, for the master of the personal put-down, and perhaps that explains Vance’s emergence as one of the administration’s chief trolls. But even if he hopes to impress President Donald Trump, Vance also appears to have a natural appetite for conflict, the product of a generation that grew up with gladiatorial political instincts. It is not enough that someone else may be wrong about policy or politics; they must be stupid, mendacious, vile or, yes, even overweight.

“Vice President Vance’s willingness publicly to disparage others in personal terms stands apart from the behavior of modern vice presidents during the last half-century,” said Joel K. Goldstein, a scholar of the vice presidency at the St. Louis University School of Law. Whatever his motivation, Goldstein added, “it departs from the norms associated with the office and undermines the goal of promoting rational public discourse.”

Vance’s advisers and allies see it differently, of course. By engaging with critics, however disparagingly, they argue that he is demonstrating the sort of accessibility and authenticity Americans are craving, at least Americans of a particular stripe. He has himself been the target of plenty of ugly attacks and should be free to push back. Those who see his tone as uncouth, they say, are the same pompous elites who have similarly tut-tutted Trump for more than a decade.

“I tend to err on the side of openness,” Vance told NBC News early last year. “That’s probably a generational thing, right? I come from a very tech-forward generation.”

Still, even Vance has evinced some concern with his online habits. In May, he told NBC that he had given up social media for Lent, deleting the app for X, formerly called Twitter, from his phone. “It’s one of these things where not having that as a distraction, I think, has made me much more productive,” he said.

But he said that living “in such a crazy bubble” meant that social media gave him a chance to have unplanned interactions with people. “I think one of the good things about social media is that it actually exposes you to unfiltered raw opinions, and that’s one of the things that I need to hear as a political leader,” he added. “So I will definitely reinstall it, but I’ve enjoyed my little break from it.”

A spokesperson for the vice president, who declined to comment on the record, said Vance’s words to NBC still stood, but that did not mean he would not engage online with supporters and critics alike.

What makes Vance’s combative tone online so striking is that it comes in contrast to other venues where he projects a more thoughtful, measured demeanor. His new book, “Communion,” released in June, offered an introspective look at his journey from evangelical Christianity to atheism to Catholicism. To promote it, he even went on ABC’s “The View” for a vigorous but civil interview with the mostly liberal hosts.

One of the hosts, Joy Behar, even said afterward that Vance had a sense of humor and that, while she disagreed with him on issues, he should run in 2028 because he would stop being so caustic. “I think if he were president, he’d go back to being a kinder person,” she said. “Trump is the one who’s not kind.”

Vice presidents have often played the role of attack dog, traditionally freer to be more aggressive than the presidents they served. The most vituperative vice president of the modern age was surely Spiro T. Agnew, who eagerly served as President Richard M. Nixon’s pit bull against perceived enemies like liberals (“pusillanimous pussyfooters”), journalists (“nattering nabobs of negativism”) and anti-war protesters (“an effete corps of impudent snobs”).

But he never had access to the bullhorn of social media. And his successors have generally taken a less abrasive, even stodgy approach, attacking opponents, yes, but steering away from the kind of personal denigration that Vance favors. Even Mike Pence, Trump’s first vice president, maintained an old-fashioned disciplined dignity throughout his four years in office, in sharp contrast to Vance’s bring-it-on feistiness.

“It’s childish behavior that is unbecoming of the office,” said Kevin Kellems, who was communications director for Vice President Dick Cheney. “He’s behaving like a high school jock trying to win over the temporary young fun friends.”

Jamal Simmons, who served as communications director for Vice President Kamala Harris, said Vance appeared to be auditioning for Trump’s support for a presidential run in 2028.

“I would guess this is the culture of Vance’s boss in grading his performance,” Simmons said. “In the Trump administration, everybody has an audience of one, and you get rewarded for being pugilistic and snarky.”

Vance certainly has the pugilistic, snarky part down. Never much of a turn-the-other-cheek kind of guy, he issued blast after blast through most of last year and into early this year until his Lenten break from social media. What makes him different from Trump, who regularly attacks friends and foes alike online, is that Vance directly responds to critical messages and gets into back-and-forth arguments with other posters.

“I have an extraordinary tolerance for disagreements and criticisms from the various people in our coalition,” he wrote last year about attacks on Tucker Carlson’s son Buckley, who works for the vice president. “But I am a very loyal person, and I have zero tolerance for scumbags attacking my staff. And yes, *everyone* who I’ve seen attack Buckley with lies is a scumbag.”

He does not hesitate to go after journalists who annoy him. Terry Moran, the former ABC News correspondent, is “a leftwing radical,” he claimed. Josh Kraushaar of the Jewish Insider, he wrote, is either “the biggest hack in Washington” or “the dumbest journalist in Washington.”

Nor does he hesitate to take on fellow Republicans. David Reaboi, whose X biography describes him as a “right-wing Twitter pugilist,” is, according to the vice president, a “loser” for suggesting that Vance’s team was leaking to the news media about Iran peace talks. Right-wing influencers like Laura Loomer, Vance wrote, are “disgraceful actually” for “attacking the administration and sowing division” in a dispute about how much to focus on abortion.

He also has little filter when it comes to profanity. “I hate this smug, self-assured bullshit,” he wrote of a podcaster who called Trump supporters “very, very dumb.” He declared a Wall Street Journal story reporting that Trump sent a bawdy letter to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to be “complete and utter bullshit.” To Democratic senators grilling Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health and human services secretary, he wrote, “You’re full of shit and everyone knows it.”

After he deleted his app for Lent, Vance’s social media feed turned more conventional, evidently maintained by his staff. For the past couple of months, it broadly praised Trump, boasted about the vice president’s anti-fraud efforts, said nice things about Vance’s wife, praised Trump some more, offered support to political allies, gave updates on Iran talks and praised Trump even more.

But then this week, the authentic Vance was clearly back online, lashing out at Marc Thiessen, a former speechwriter for President George W. Bush and columnist for The Washington Post who has been one of the leading voices on the right supporting Trump’s war against Iran.

In a scathing column last week, Thiessen blamed the vice president for the failed memorandum of understanding with Tehran and said Vance “publicly undermines the president” by seemingly contradicting Trump’s stated policy. “Perhaps it’s time for the president to take the advice of those who have delivered him success in Iran — not those like Vance who have failed him,” Thiessen wrote.

A few days later, Thiessen jumped into an unrelated social media thread over affordability — specifically, the price of burritos. Responding to a post quoting a university student complaining that it costs too much to buy Mexican fast food, Thiessen wrote, “Cry me a river. The burritos in the college cafeteria are included in your meal plan.”

That was when Vance jumped in, suggesting that Thiessen had gone back for seconds in the cafeteria too often. Some commenters online came to Thiessen’s defense by recalling that Vance, who by his own account lost 30 pounds between 2022 and 2024, was not always so svelte himself.

Thiessen did not respond to messages requesting comment, and Vance’s office declined to elaborate.

An ally of the vice president said the columnist had it coming. “It’s neither appropriate nor constructive for self-described ‘Republican’ commentators like Marc Thiessen, who earns an absurd living promoting war after war on television, to use their platforms to dismiss the economic anxieties of young Americans,” said Alex Bruesewitz, a former Trump campaign aide.

He added, “I support elected officials who speak the truth. The vice president was right: Marc Thiessen appears to be severely obese. He should lay off the burritos.”

But don’t expect Vance to lay off the social media.
